title: What Rust doesn't have
intro: Some things you reach for by habit do not exist in Rust: `x++`, `a ? b : c`, `null`, C-style `for`, default arguments, classes, exceptions, `goto`. Each one fails with a compiler message, and each has a Rust way. This page lists them, with the real error and what to write instead.

coming_from.go: `i++` is a statement in Go, and Rust has no `++` at all. Much else matches: Go has no ternary operator, no function overloading by type, no default arguments and no mixing of typed number types either. What you give up is `nil`, `goto`, `defer`, `for cond {}` and the `if err != nil` boilerplate: Rust has `Option`, labeled `break`, `Drop`, `while` and `?`. Watch the `break` inside a `switch`: in Rust it leaves the loop.
coming_from.kotlin: You are used to a lot of this already: `if` is an expression, there is no ternary operator, and `T?` is a checked null. What Rust takes away is `++`, `?.`, `?:` and `!!` (`Option` has `map`, `unwrap_or` and `unwrap`), default and named arguments, `open` classes with inheritance, and exceptions (`Result` and `?` replace `try`/`catch`).
coming_from.python: Python has no `x++` either, so `x += 1` is already your habit. What is new is that an `if` needs a `bool` (an empty list or a `0` is not false), a call has no keyword arguments and a definition has no default values, `//` starts a comment, `and`/`or`/`not`/`elif` are `&&`/`||`/`!`/`else if`, a name has one type, and braces replace the indentation.
coming_from.typescript: `x++`, `a ? b : c`, `null` and `undefined`, `??`, truthiness (`if (name)`), `throw` and optional parameters all have a different Rust form: `x += 1`, `if a { b } else { c }`, `Option`, `unwrap_or`, an explicit test, `Result` and `?`, and a struct. Careful: `u?.name` is valid Rust, and it is not a safe call but an early return. Rust also does not turn a number into another number type for you.
coming_from.java: `i++`, `?:`, `null`, `new`, `this`, `extends`, function overloading, `switch` that falls through, `finally` and checked or unchecked exceptions all have a different Rust form. Java widens `int` to `long` on its own; Rust makes you write the conversion. A `break` in a `switch` inside a loop leaves the `switch` in Java; in Rust it leaves the loop.
coming_from.csharp: `i++`, `?:`, `?.`, `new`, `this`, `: BaseClass`, function overloads, optional and named arguments, and `try`/`catch` have a different Rust form, and `null` becomes `Option`. C# widens `int` to `long` on its own; Rust makes you write the conversion. A `break` in a `switch` inside a loop leaves the `switch` in C#; in Rust it leaves the loop.
coming_from.c: `i++`, `?:`, `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)`, `NULL`, a `switch` that falls through, `goto`, `(double)n`, `->` and `#define` do not exist or fail in Rust, as does `if (n)` on a number. A global you assign without `unsafe` fails to compile too, and C's silent number conversions (`int n = 3.9;`) need an explicit `as`. A `break;` at the end of a ported `case` compiles and leaves the loop.
coming_from.cpp: Everything in the C list, plus classes with inheritance, function overloads, default arguments, constructors and exceptions: Rust has none of them. A `struct` holds data, an `impl` block holds methods, a trait shares behaviour (and `impl Add` is your `operator+`), a `Drop` runs where a destructor would, and a `Result` carries a failure. `auto` is `let`.

notes: Rust has no `x++` and no `a ? b : c`. Write `x += 1`, and `if a { b } else { c }`, which is an expression.
There is no `null`. A value that may be missing has the type `Option<T>`, and the compiler makes you handle `None`.
Numbers do not convert on their own: `i32` plus `i64` is an error. Write `as`, `From` or `try_from`.

No `switch` fallthrough, no exceptions for ordinary errors, no default or named arguments, no function overloading by parameter type, no classes and no `goto`. Each has a Rust form, shown on this page. A `break` in a `match` inside a loop leaves the loop.

gotcha.title: Writing x++
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Java, C, C++, C#, Kotlin and JavaScript, `count++` adds one, and it reads the same in all of them.
gotcha.rust_sees: Rust has no `++` or `--` operator. `count++` is not a statement the parser knows, and the compiler stops with a message that says so and shows `count += 1`.
gotcha.why: The compiler recognises the habit and names it: "Rust has no postfix increment operator". The fix is `count += 1`. Python is the other language here with no `++` operator. Elsewhere `++` is part of the language: Go allows it only as a statement, and the others also allow it inside larger expressions.

go.says: Go prints 3. `count++` is a statement, not an expression, so `x := count++` is an error in Go. `++count` does not exist.

kotlin.says: Kotlin prints 3. `count++` and `++count` both work, and can sit inside a larger expression.

python.says: Python refuses with a `SyntaxError`: it has no `++` operator, so write `count += 1`. It is the one language here with no `++`. Note that `++count` and `--count` are legal in Python and do nothing: they read as `+(+count)` and `-(-count)`.
python.code:
count = 0
for _ in range(3):
    count++
print(f"count: {count}")
python.out:
File "main.py", line 3
    count++
           ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

typescript.says: TypeScript prints 3. `count++` and `++count` work, as in JavaScript, and `--count` decrements. In Rust `--count` compiles and negates twice.

java.says: Java prints 3. `count++` and `++count` work, also inside expressions such as `a[i++]`.

csharp.says: C# prints 3. `count++` and `++count` work, also inside expressions.

c.says: C prints 3. `count++` works, also inside expressions such as `a[i++]`.

cpp.says: C++ prints 3. `count++` and `++count` work, and they can be overloaded for your own types.

assert label == "big"

# truthiness: empty and zero values count as false
assert not []
assert not ""
assert not 0
assert not None
assert [0]

# keyword and default arguments

assert area(width=3, height=4) == 12

# floor division, power, chained comparison, in, is
assert 7 // 2 == 3 and -7 // 2 == -4
assert 2**10 == 1024
n = 3
assert 1 < n < 5
assert n in [1, 2, 3]
assert None is None
assert True and not False

# an empty string is falsy, so `or` replaces it too
assert ("" or "Hello") == "Hello"

# and, or, not
assert (True and not False) or False

# one value can be an int or a float, and a function takes any type
assert 1 + 2.5 == 3.5
assert 1 == 1.0
assert double(2) == 4 and double("ab") == "abab"

# a name can change type

z = "a"
assert z == "a"

    assert False, "no exception"
except ValueError:
    caught = True
assert caught

    case 3:
        out = "three"
assert out == "small"

def visit():
    global visits
    visits += 1


visit()
assert visits == 1
